entries.title: Every recorded song holds two separate copyrights
entries.take: The song (music and lyrics) and the recording of it are two works, each with its own owner and its own income.
entries.body: A song is a musical work. A recording of someone performing it is a sound recording. US law treats them as distinct works, and a registration for one does not cover the other. Royalty systems follow the same split, which is why one stream can create payments to more than one set of people.
do: Write down who owns the song and who owns the recording for every release.

entries.title: Musical work (the song)
entries.take: The composition: the music plus any words that go with it. Songwriters, composers and their publishers own and collect on it.

entries.title: Sound recording (the master)
entries.take: A work made by fixing a series of sounds, such as a recorded performance. In US law it excludes sounds that accompany a film or other audiovisual work.

entries.title: Who owns a recording: performers and producers, unless it is for hire
entries.take: The Copyright Office names the featured performer and the producer as the authors of a recording, with an employer or commissioning party as author in work-made-for-hire cases.
entries.body: That is the starting point in US registration practice. In real deals ownership is often moved by contract, so the owner on paper can differ from the author. Read the agreement for each release, and have a music lawyer review anything that transfers ownership.
do: Check each contract for who owns the master and for how long.

entries.title: Mistake: registering the song and assuming the recording is covered
entries.take: A registration for a song covers its music and lyrics, not the recorded performance. Recordings are normally registered on their own.
entries.body: The Copyright Office says the two are usually registered separately, with narrow cases where one application can cover both. The same habit shows up at royalty bodies: a song registration does not put the recording on file, and the reverse is also true.
do: Check separately that the song and the recording are each on file.
Read Circular 50 and Circular 56 before filing.

entries.title: Copyright protection starts on creation; registration is a separate step
entries.take: In the US a recording is protected from the moment it is fixed. Registering with the Copyright Office is a separate step with its own form, fee and deposit.
entries.body: Circular 56 says neither registration nor publication is needed for protection under current law. Circulars 50 and 56 explain how to apply: a completed application, a fee that changes over time, and a copy of the work. Check the Office's current fee schedule before you file.
do: Read the circular for your type of work before applying.

entries.title: Income streams and who collects each in the US
entries.take: A song and a recording earn through different rights, and different bodies collect them. This table covers the main US routes.
rows: Streams and downloads of the song
Radio, TV, venues, streams as performances
A performing rights society (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR)
Copies, deals and licences from the recording owner
The label or distributor, by contract
Publishers or their licensing agents (ask yours)

entries.title: Mechanical and performance royalties pay for different uses
entries.take: A mechanical royalty pays for making copies of a song, and a performance royalty pays when it is performed or communicated to the public.
entries.body: Both terms come from industry custom more than from statute. WIPO describes the mechanical right as the right to record a work and distribute copies, and the performing right as covering live or broadcast use and other ways of reaching the public. A single stream of a song can involve both rights, so more than one body may collect on it.
do: Register each song with every body that collects on it.

entries.title: Mechanical right
entries.take: The right to record a song and to make and distribute copies of that recording. Digital streams and downloads count as copies for US mechanical licensing.

entries.title: Performing right
entries.take: The right to perform a song publicly, or to authorise others to. The US statute treats a performance as public at an open place or when sent to the public.

entries.title: US recordings have no general public performance right
entries.take: A US sound recording owner has a performance right only for digital audio transmissions, not the broader right that song owners hold.
entries.body: Section 114 leaves out section 106(4) for sound recordings and keeps clause (6), the digital audio transmission right. This is why the US recording side has one dedicated route for digital performance, and why outside the US, where neighbouring rights work differently, the money looks different.
do: Do not assume a UK or Canadian recording royalty has a US equivalent.

entries.title: Sync licences need permission for the song and for the recording
entries.take: Putting music in a video, ad or game is a negotiated licence. If an existing recording is used, the song owner and the recording owner each have to agree.
entries.body: Sync fees are set by deal, not by a fixed rate, and are paid to the owners of each work, not collected by a society. Because the song and the recording are separate works, one licence for one side does not cover the other. A music lawyer should review a sync deal.
do: Ask the owner of each side for a written licence before the music is used.

entries.title: Printed music and lyrics are another reproduction use
entries.take: Printed sheet music counts as a reproduction of the song. Lyrics are part of the song, so using them is also a use of the song.
entries.body: WIPO lists printed sheet music among the forms of reproduction of a musical work, and the Copyright Office describes a musical composition as music with any lyrics. Print and lyrics licensing is usually a smaller income stream, handled by publishers and their licensing partners.
do: Ask your publisher or administrator whether print and lyric licensing is included.

entries.title: Neighbouring (related) rights
entries.take: Rights held by performers, record producers and broadcasters, separate from the song's copyright. Many countries pay them when recordings are broadcast or played in public.

entries.title: Music collected by CISAC societies in 2022
entries.take: CISAC societies collected EUR 10.83 bn for music in 2022, before costs are deducted. It covers songs, not recordings.

entries.title: Digital was 35% of all CISAC collections in 2022
entries.unit: percent of EUR 12.1 bn, all repertoires, 2022
entries.take: Digital income reached EUR 4.17 bn, about a third of all CISAC society collections across every repertoire in 2022.

entries.title: The MLC collects US digital mechanicals for songs
entries.take: The MLC collects mechanical royalties from eligible US streaming and download services under the blanket licence, then pays the song's owners.
entries.body: The Copyright Office designated the MLC for this job. Services send the MLC usage data and money each month. The MLC matches usage to registered songs and pays self-administered writers, publishers, administrators and foreign societies. Songs that are not registered or matched can hold unpaid money.
do: Register your songs with the MLC, or confirm your publisher has.

entries.title: Performing rights societies collect for public performance of songs
entries.take: In the US, ASCAP, BMI and SESAC license public performance of songs for their members, and GMR works as a fourth.
entries.body: The statute describes a performing rights society as a body licensing public performance of non-dramatic musical works for owners, naming ASCAP, BMI and SESAC. Songview, a shared system of those societies, reconciles their ownership data.
do: Join one society as a writer and register each song with it.

entries.title: SoundExchange collects digital performance money for recordings
entries.take: SoundExchange pays recording owners and artists for digital play on non-interactive services, but only those who have registered with it.
entries.body: SoundExchange names services such as SiriusXM and Pandora, and says artists and owners must register to be paid. It keeps lists of unregistered creators. Registering is free. What these services pay per play is decided by the Copyright Royalty Board.
do: Register as artist and, if you own the master, as a recording owner.

entries.title: Labels and distributors pay recording income by contract
entries.take: Outside the statutory digital performance licence, a featured artist is paid by the recording owner under their contract.
entries.body: Section 114(g) says such an artist is entitled to payments from the owner as the artist's contract provides. WIPO notes record companies sign direct contracts with performers. Which party pays, and what it deducts, depends on the deal, so ask a music lawyer to review it.
do: Ask your label or distributor for the statement terms in writing.

entries.title: A song's income divides into a writer share and a publisher share
entries.take: Many societies pay a work's income to the composer and the publisher separately, in proportions set by their contract or society rules.
entries.body: WIPO says a typical work has two parties with a claim, the composer and the publisher, and that the division follows the contract between them, the rules of the society, or both. This guide does not state a standard percentage; check your agreement and your society's rules.
do: Read your publishing contract and your society's rules for the split.

entries.title: Writer's share and publisher's share
entries.take: The two parts into which a song's income is divided. The writer's share is paid to the writer and the publisher's share to the publisher or administrator.

entries.title: A publisher licenses songs and pays advances
entries.take: A music publisher gets the right to license a writer's songs, collects the income, and often pays an advance that is later recovered from royalties.
entries.body: WIPO describes publishers as the link that brings songs to record and broadcast companies and as a source of advances to writers. The writer is paid a share of what the publisher receives. Terms vary, and a music lawyer should read any publishing deal before it is signed.
do: Ask what the publisher does for the share it keeps.

entries.title: Publishing administrator
entries.take: A company that registers songs, collects income and keeps records for a rights owner, for a fee, without owning the songs. It differs from a publisher that owns a share.

entries.title: Mistake: registering shares that add up to more than 100 percent
entries.take: An overclaim occurs when the shares filed for a song at the MLC add up to more than 100 percent.
entries.body: The MLC says an overclaim should be resolved promptly so payments are accurate, and it provides a tool for amending or relinquishing shares and sharing evidence. Agree each co-writer's split before registering, and use the same split everywhere.
do: Agree and record each co-writer's percentage before you register.

entries.title: Statutory digital performance split for recordings, as the law states it
entries.take: Section 114(g) divides the statutory digital performance receipts four ways. It does not cover other income from a recording.
rows: A fund run with the AFM

entries.title: Registrations for a songwriter and for an artist
entries.take: Each kind of money has its own register. Tick what applies to you and check it separately; one registration does not cover another.

groups.name: If you write songs
items: A performing rights society, as a writer
Each song at the MLC, directly or through a publisher or administrator
Songs you share: written agreement on every split
Your details in the ASCAP and BMI public searches

entries.title: Register a song before it earns
entries.take: Register the song with your society and the MLC, then check the matching and the public databases.
entries.body: The MLC lets members register songs one by one, in bulk or by CWR files, and advises checking its claiming tool first because someone may already have registered the song. Once registered, watch the matching tool as new recording data arrives.
do: Search the MLC's public tool before adding a song.
Register the song, then confirm the shares match everywhere.

entries.title: Register the recording when it is released
entries.take: Register with SoundExchange, give the recording an ISRC, and link it to the song so the song's owners are paid.
entries.body: SoundExchange says artists and owners must register to receive digital performance money. PPL explains that an ISRC identifies a recording, with 12 characters including a code for the rightsholder. The MLC's matching tool lets users connect recordings to songs.
do: Register with SoundExchange for each role you hold.
Check the match to the song in the MLC Matching Tool.

entries.title: ISRC code
entries.take: International Standard Recording Code: a 12-character identifier for one recording, made of a rightsholder code, a year and a five-digit number.

entries.title: ISWC code
entries.take: International Standard Musical Work Code: a number that identifies a song and links it to its rights holders in the society systems.

entries.title: Mistake: registering with one body and thinking all the money is covered
entries.take: SoundExchange, the MLC and a performing rights society each pay for different rights. A registration at one does not trigger payment from another.
entries.body: A writer-artist can be owed from several places: songs from a society and the MLC, recordings from SoundExchange. Each pays only those who are on its books, so a gap in one register stays a gap.
do: Use the checklist on this page and tick each register separately.

entries.title: Pre-1972 recordings and producer letters of direction have their own rules
entries.take: Recordings from before 15 February 1972 have federal remedies under Title II, and producers can be paid through a letter of direction under Title III.
entries.body: Title II covers sound recordings fixed before that date and relies on schedules filed with the Copyright Office. Title III lets a collective accept written instructions to pay producers, mixers and engineers a share of statutory digital performance money. Neither is covered here; see their own pages.
do: Look at the Copyright Office's Title II and Title III pages.

entries.title: Who collects what in the UK, Canada and Germany
entries.take: A basic map of bodies with pages read for this guide. Other countries and rights are not shown, and rules differ by body.
rows: Check the society for your territory (not read here)
Check the local body (not read here)

entries.title: Societies work abroad through reciprocal agreements
entries.take: A society licenses mainly at home. To be paid abroad, societies appoint each other, so foreign income reaches you through your own society.
entries.body: WIPO describes reciprocal representation agreements, under which each society licenses the other's repertoire in its own country and then passes on the money. Because of this, a writer's registration at home matters for income earned in other countries.
do: Confirm that your society collects abroad on your behalf.

entries.title: Outside the US, recordings can earn neighbouring rights money
entries.take: In the UK and Canada, bodies such as PPL and Re:Sound collect on recordings and pay rightsholders and performers. It is a separate account from songwriter income.
entries.body: PPL says rightsholders can ask it to collect international royalties, and Re:Sound tells those who performed on or made released recordings that they may be owed. A US artist should check, per country, who collects and what registration is needed.
do: Register with PPL or Re:Sound if your recordings are played in those countries.

entries.title: PPL divides UK recording money between rightsholders and performers
entries.take: PPL matches reported plays against its database of more than 28 million recordings, then pays half to rightsholders and half to qualifying performers.
entries.body: A performer must qualify for a track before the performer share is paid; if not, that portion goes to the rightsholder. Several performers on one recording share by agreement or PPL's allocation policy. The share is often called equitable remuneration.
do: Check in myPPL that you are credited on each recording.

entries.title: Society reports show what was collected, not what was paid
entries.take: CISAC's collection totals are gross, before societies deduct costs. Deductions can include running costs and, in many societies, cultural or social funds.
entries.body: WIPO says societies may deduct administration costs and other charges before distributing. CISAC states that its figures are gross collections. So a large headline number does not show what writers and publishers receive.
do: Read your society's distribution rules for deductions.

entries.title: How money moves from a stream to a songwriter
entries.take: A service reports a play and pays a collective. The collective matches it to registered owners and pays them. A publisher then pays the writer under their deal.
entries.body: For digital mechanicals, the MLC receives monthly usage and money, matches it, and pays members. For performance money the society does the same for its members. If a publisher is involved, the writer's share reaches the writer under the contract. Unmatched money stays unpaid.
do: Check each step: registered, matched, and paid to the right account.

entries.title: How money moves from a stream to an artist
entries.take: Digital performance money goes through SoundExchange and is split by statute. Other recording income goes to the owner, who pays the artist as agreed.
entries.body: Section 114(g)(2) sets the split for money collected under the statutory licence. Section 114(g)(1) says outside that licence the artist is paid under the artist's contract. A label or distributor usually receives the streaming income, and the deal fixes the artist's share and deductions.
do: Ask for the royalty statement that shows each source of income.

entries.title: Form W-8BEN: a form that non-US payees may be asked to give
entries.take: A foreign individual who owns income subject to US withholding gives Form W-8BEN to the payer when asked. It is not tax advice.
entries.body: The IRS says the payer or withholding agent receives the form on request, whether or not the person is claiming a reduced rate or an exemption. What rate applies and whether a tax treaty helps depends on the person's situation, so speak to a tax adviser.
do: Ask the payer which form it needs.
Ask a tax adviser how US withholding applies to you.

entries.title: Mistake: leaving tax details out of payee accounts
entries.take: A payee account without current tax details can slow or reduce payment. The MLC tells members to refresh their bank and tax paperwork.
entries.body: The MLC's tools page reminds members to keep contact, bank and tax information current in their member settings so they receive what they are owed. The same habit applies at any payer. Tax rules vary, so ask a tax adviser about yours.
do: Check tax and bank details in each payee account each year.

usco-mma.title: The Music Modernization Act (overview page)
usco-mma.support: Three titles; MLC designated to collect and distribute mechanicals; from 1 January 2021 songwriters and publishers register with the MLC portal to be paid under the blanket license.

mlc-tools.title: The MLC's Tools
mlc-tools.support: Public Work Search (more than 55 million songs), Claiming, Works Registration, Matching, Overclaims, Catalog Export and Transfer tools; check the Claiming Tool before registering; keep banking and tax details current.

wipo-cmo-music.title: Educational Material on Collective Management of Copyright and Related Rights, Module 2: Management of copyright and related rights in the field of music
wipo-cmo-music.support: Sec. 3.6: social and cultural deductions common in many countries, not cost cover, must be agreed in advance with rights holders and other CMOs; sec. 3.7: ISWC is an ISO work number linked to rights holders in the IPI system; reciprocal agreements.

cisac-gcr-2023.title: Global Collections Report 2023 (for 2022 data)
cisac-gcr-2023.support: Music collections EUR 10.83 bn in 2022, up 28.0%; About the report: gross collections before deductions for administrative, cultural or social purposes; 225 members in 116 countries or territories.

sx-owed.title: Artists, Labels & Producers
sx-owed.support: 'Are you owed royalties?': artists and recording owners must register to be paid; search tool; four status lists and what each means; registering free; SX Direct to search and claim. No claim deadline.

cmrra-unclaimed.title: Unclaimed Works Portal for Online Music Services
cmrra-unclaimed.support: CMRRA Direct account needed (approval up to 3 business days); match recordings and add missing shares via the Unclaimed Works menu; quarterly invoicing for past and current use; no fee or deadline. Read with WebFetch.

ppl-performers.title: Performers
ppl-performers.support: Audible contributions count; some roles non-payable; myPPL line-up claim, evidence; missing track: ask rightsholder; studio producer only if directing live performance, own form signed by featured performers; over 28 million tracks.

usc-101.publisher: United States Congress (Cornell LII copy of the U.S. Code)
usc-101.title: 17 U.S.C. 101: Definitions
usc-101.support: Definitions of sound recordings, phonorecords, joint work, work made for hire, perform publicly, and performing rights society (names ASCAP, BMI, SESAC).
usc-101.edition: Title 17, section 101, as shown by LII

usc-106.publisher: United States Congress (Cornell LII copy of the U.S. Code)
usc-106.title: 17 U.S.C. 106: Exclusive rights in copyrighted works
usc-106.support: Clause (1) reproduce, (3) distribute, (4) perform musical works publicly, (6) perform sound recordings publicly by digital audio transmission.
usc-106.edition: Title 17, section 106, as shown by LII

usc-114.publisher: United States Congress (Cornell LII copy of the U.S. Code)
usc-114.title: 17 U.S.C. 114: Scope of exclusive rights in sound recordings
usc-114.support: (a) no section 106(4) right for sound recordings; (g)(1) artist payments by contract outside the statutory licence; (g)(2) 50 / 2.5 / 2.5 / 45 percent split; letters of direction.
usc-114.edition: Title 17, section 114, as shown by LII

circ-50.title: Circular 50: Copyright Registration for Musical Compositions
circ-50.support: Song and recording are separate works; a song registration covers music and lyrics, not the recorded performance; application, fee and deposit; author of the song.

circ-56.title: Circular 56: Copyright Registration for Sound Recordings
circ-56.support: Sound recording defined; distinct from underlying song and from phonorecord; authors are featured performer and producer unless work made for hire; registration not required for protection; digital performance right only.

usco-pre1972.title: Classics Protection and Access Act (Title II of the Music Modernization Act)
usco-pre1972.support: Federal remedies for unauthorized use of sound recordings fixed before 15 February 1972; schedules filed with the Office; term and transition periods.

irs-w8ben.title: About Form W-8 BEN, Certificate of Foreign Status of Beneficial Owner for United States Tax Withholding and Reporting (Individuals)
irs-w8ben.support: A foreign person who is beneficial owner of an amount subject to withholding gives the form to the withholding agent or payer when requested, whether or not claiming a reduced rate or exemption.

songview.title: Songview
songview.support: Shared copyright data for over 40 million musical works; ingests ownership data from each PRO, reconciles it by agreed rules, sends it back to ASCAP and BMI public databases.

mlc-home.title: The MLC (home page)
mlc-home.support: Administers blanket mechanical licenses for eligible streaming and download services in the US; collects, matches registered songs, pays monthly; market share distributions begin April 2027.

ppl-calc.title: How royalties are calculated
ppl-calc.support: UK public play and broadcast money: one half to the recording rightsholder, one half to qualifying performers (equitable remuneration); PPL repertoire database 28 million recordings; international agreements with CMOs.

ppl-rrh.title: Recording rightsholders
ppl-rrh.support: Who can join as a rightsholder; ISRC structure of 12 characters; PPL is the UK ISRC agency; international collection can be requested after joining.

socan.title: SOCAN (home page)
socan.support: Licenses music and collects and distributes royalties in Canada and abroad; manages performing and reproduction rights; serves creators and publishers.

resound.title: Re:Sound Music Licensing Company (home page)
resound.support: Canadian not-for-profit that licenses performance rights for artists and record companies; those who performed on or made released recordings may be owed royalties.

gema.title: GEMA: For composers, lyricists and music publishers
gema.support: German society for composers, lyricists and publishers; over 100,000 members; members register works and are paid when works are performed or reproduced.
